name: Anti-inflammatory diet
lead: An anti-inflammatory diet is an eating pattern built around the idea that what a person eats can raise or lower the body's low-grade inflammatory activity. It emphasises whole foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols and fibre, and limits processed foods, refined carbohydrates, sugary drinks and red and processed meat.[11][14] There is no single official version; the Mediterranean diet is most often given as the model.[11][20]

People adopt it for how they look as well as how they feel. Proponents connect it to clearer-looking skin, less facial puffiness, easier fat loss, more comfortable joints for training and recovery, and healthier skin with age. The chain is indirect: food pattern, then inflammatory signals, body weight and gut and joint comfort, then the skin, leanness and training capacity people care about.[11][21]

Research on the diet is mostly framed around disease: inflammation biomarkers, heart disease, bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, depression and cognitive health. Randomized trials have tested anti-inflammatory menus in rheumatoid arthritis and ulcerative colitis, and a scoring tool, the Dietary Inflammatory Index, is used to rate diets in observational studies.[7][8][15][16] Trials of the diet on acne or facial puffiness have not been published.

paras: Proponents prioritise fatty fish, berries, leafy and cruciferous vegetables, extra-virgin olive oil and nuts, and avoid fried foods, sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates; Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, describes the aim as lowering markers such as CRP and IL-6.[11] A British Journal of Nutrition review characterises the diet as incorporating fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, legumes, spices, herbs and plant-based protein while limiting red and processed meat, refined carbohydrates and saturated fats.[14]

Harvard Health Publishing, in a page reviewed in 2026 that quotes nutrition epidemiologist Frank Hu, lists tomatoes, olive oil, leafy greens, nuts, fatty fish and fruit such as berries, cherries and oranges as foods associated with lower inflammation. It lists refined carbohydrates, fried food, sugary drinks, red and processed meat, and margarine, shortening and lard as foods associated with more. The page presents these links as based on experimental and observational studies and notes that the food and inflammation link persisted after accounting for obesity.[21]

Many descriptions are close to the Mediterranean diet, which Wikipedia says was proposed as a concept in 1975 by Ancel and Margaret Keys, based on eating patterns in Greece, southern Italy and the Mediterranean coasts of France and Spain observed in the late 1950s and early 1960s, with olive oil as the main fat and low amounts of red meat, processed meat and sweets.[20] Other patterns in the same family include plant-based, high-fibre and DASH-style diets, which a 2025 review groups among the patterns with the strongest support for lipid management.[18]

The proposed mechanism is that chronic low-grade inflammation contributes to many diseases and that eating patterns can raise or lower inflammatory signals. A British Journal of Nutrition review describes pathways linking systemic inflammation, food choices and conditions including obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, autoinflammatory disease, cancer and cognitive disorders, and identifies food-derived bioactive compounds said to modulate them.[14]

The Dietary Inflammatory Index is a scoring tool that rates the inflammatory potential of a diet; it has been related to cardiovascular and colorectal outcomes in meta-analyses.[2][4] A systematic review of observational studies found associations between dietary patterns and inflammation biomarkers in adults.[10] A cardiology review describes how highly processed, calorie-dense diets cause spikes in post-meal glucose and lipids that increase oxidant stress and inflammation, and discusses dietary strategies to lessen them.[1]
A review in Nutrients describes the diet as modulating gut microbiota and helping control obesity, one route by which proponents expect it to change body composition.[17]

In appearance communities, an anti-inflammatory diet is cited for reducing acne, redness and puffiness by cutting sugar and processed food. These are community claims; trials of an anti-inflammatory diet on acne or facial puffiness have not been published.

A review describes the anti-inflammatory diet as modulating the gut microbiota and controlling obesity, and the Mediterranean diet may help overweight adults reduce calorie intake and lose weight, with weight loss similar to other diets in a 2016 review cited by Wikipedia.[17][20] A lifter on a T Nation forum wrote that moving to a carnivore or keto style of eating, which he called anti-inflammatory, helped him shed weight in his own experience.[29]

Lifters sometimes adopt anti-inflammatory eating or supplements for joint comfort and recovery. A forum user advises that after 40, choices such as fish oil and curcumin may support staying leaner and more muscular, while Wikipedia notes a 2019 meta-analysis found curcumin did not significantly lower several circulating inflammatory markers.[19][12] Research on joints comes from rheumatoid arthritis, not from athletes (see Clinical studies).

In general terms, people following the pattern build meals around vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, fish, nuts and olive oil, and replace pastries, fried food and sweetened drinks.[21][14] Some versions add herbs and spices such as turmeric and ginger, green tea, or probiotics and fibre-rich foods; clinical trials have used structured menu plans designed by dietitians, such as plans raising fibre, antioxidants, probiotics and omega-3 intake in the ulcerative colitis study.[16] Others in strength and bodybuilding forums combine the pattern with fish oil or curcumin supplements.[19] Because there is no standard definition, the foods and rules differ between books, clinics and online communities.

In rheumatoid arthritis, the ADIRA randomized, single-blinded crossover trial tested an anti-inflammatory diet against a control diet and reported effects on disease activity.[15] A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of potentially anti-inflammatory diets (Mediterranean, vegetarian, vegan, ketogenic) on pain searched databases through November 2021, found 564 unique publications, included 12 in the review and 7 in the meta-analysis, and reported that all studies had high risk of bias, with the authors concluding that anti-inflammatory diets were associated with lower pain.[13] A Mediterranean diet and activity-nudge randomized trial in women with rheumatoid arthritis (MADEIRA) was also published, and a study of a low arachidonic acid diet with fish oil in rheumatoid arthritis appeared in 2003.[24][9]

In ulcerative colitis, a randomized 6-month open-label trial compared an anti-inflammatory diet with Canada's Food Guide in patients in remission and reported subclinical colonic inflammation and metabolomic differences.[16] A randomized trial of faecal microbiota transplantation combined with an anti-inflammatory diet reported outcomes over one year, a case series covered inflammatory bowel disease, and a transcriptomics study examined a Mediterranean-inspired diet in Crohn's disease.[5][6][28] A review covered nutrition and gut microbiota in IBD.[3]

A meta-analysis of Dietary Inflammatory Index studies associated more inflammatory diets with cardiovascular risk and mortality (14 studies), and another with colorectal cancer risk (nine studies).[2][4] A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies with 101,950 participants found a pro-inflammatory diet associated with higher odds of depression or depressive symptoms (odds ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.62) relative to an anti-inflammatory diet.[8] A randomized trial in diabetic patients with depression tested an anti-inflammatory diet alone or with acupuncture, and a 2025 randomized trial combined an anti-inflammatory diet with probiotics in autism spectrum disorder.[26][25] A review covered dietary patterns and cognitive health in older adults.[7]

Reviews have also examined the diet in other conditions: fibromyalgia, where a 2024 review covered anti-inflammatory and gluten-free diets alongside lifestyle changes, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis, where a 2022 overview said a protective effect of an anti-inflammatory diet has been suggested while no specific diet is recommended.[22][23] A 2025 review of dyslipidemia management included the anti-inflammatory diet among patterns with the best evidence for lipid management, and a pediatric review described a children's version of the diet.[18][27] No studies on acne or facial puffiness were found.

The topic appears in mainstream health media, university health newsletters and wellness books, and in fitness forums where it is used loosely to mean eating whole foods and avoiding processed ones.[21][19] Wikipedia's page on anti-inflammatory substances treats the topic mainly through drugs and supplements, noting mixed omega-3 results and the 2019 curcumin meta-analysis, which shows how the phrase covers both diets and supplements in popular use.[12]

Because it is a food pattern rather than a drug, the diet has no dosing or labelled adverse-effect profile. People with medical conditions, such as the arthritis or bowel disease populations studied in trials, are generally managed by clinicians, and the trials above were run under clinical supervision. Grokipedia's overview advises that individual responses vary and that changes be discussed with a healthcare provider.[11]

lore.intro: The diet is discussed in appearance and fitness communities as a way to avoid processed foods for less puffiness, clearer skin, leanness and better recovery; users often pair it with supplements such as fish oil and curcumin, and some use the label for carnivore or keto eating.[19][29]

claims.claim: Cutting processed food reduces facial puffiness and acne.
claims.believers: Proponents say removing sugar and processed foods lowers inflammation visible in the face, making skin clearer and the face less swollen.
claims.experts: Published work links inflammatory diet scores and patterns with disease risks and markers; trials on acne or puffiness were not found.[2][10]

claims.believers: Users say whole-food, high-fibre eating makes it easier to lose fat and stay lean.
claims.experts: A review describes anti-inflammatory eating as modulating the gut microbiota and controlling obesity, and Mediterranean-style eating has produced weight loss similar to other diets.[17][20]

claims.claim: Anti-inflammatory eating eases joint pain and speeds recovery.
claims.believers: Lifters report that fish, olive oil and vegetables settle joints and soreness.
claims.experts: Trials in rheumatoid arthritis have studied anti-inflammatory diets for disease activity and pain; studies in healthy lifters were not found.[15][13]

claims.claim: Curcumin and fish oil supplements add an anti-inflammatory effect.
claims.believers: A forum user lists fish oil and curcumin among anti-inflammatory supplements for staying lean and muscular after 40.[19]
claims.experts: A 2019 meta-analysis found curcumin did not significantly lower circulating inflammatory markers, and omega-3 results have been inconsistent.[12]

claims.claim: A carnivore or keto diet is 'anti-inflammatory' and helps shed weight.
claims.believers: A T Nation forum user wrote that carnivore and keto accounts of healing from ailments led him to try the diet, and that its anti-inflammatory effect helped him lose weight.[29]
claims.experts: Published anti-inflammatory diet trials and the Dietary Inflammatory Index research centre on plant-rich, Mediterranean-style patterns; carnivore diets are not among the patterns those trials tested.[14][15][16]

claims.claim: Eating anti-inflammatory foods can help depression and mood.
claims.believers: Proponents of the diet say inflammation links gut, brain and mood, so food changes may support mental wellbeing.
claims.experts: A 2019 meta-analysis of observational studies reported a pro-inflammatory diet associated with higher odds of depression (OR 1.40), and a 2025 randomized trial tested the diet in diabetic patients with depression.[8][26]

card.summary: Whole-food, low-processed eating aimed at inflammation: research targets disease markers, not puffiness or acne.

quick.overview:
An anti-inflammatory diet emphasises fish, berries, greens, olive oil and nuts and limits processed food and sugar. Appearance communities cite it for less puffiness and acne.

Studies look at inflammation markers and disease; none test facial outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that diet changes lower chronic low-grade inflammation, measured by markers such as CRP and IL-6.
quick.risks: Generally a conventional food pattern; individual conditions should be discussed with a clinician, as sources advise.

chain: Eat whole, omega-3 and fibre-rich foods; cut processed foods
Lower inflammatory markers and calorie density
Clearer skin, less puffiness, leaner body, more comfortable joints for training
angle.text: People use an anti-inflammatory diet as a food-based way to support skin, leanness and recovery. The diet changes what is on the plate; effects on appearance are mediated by weight, blood sugar, gut and joint outcomes, and individuals report different results.
